working_title: Push Trolley or Electric Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses and Your Budget
angle: Most UK golfers upgrading from carrying face the same fork in the road: spend £150-£200 on a solid push trolley or three-to-five times as much on an electric. This post cuts through the noise by mapping the real decision factors (course terrain, how often you play, car-boot space, budget) to the right choice — rather than simply declaring one type the winner.
research_notes:
- Two dominant trolley types in the UK market: push (manual three-wheel) and electric (motor + lithium battery); a third 'follow/remote' tier sits at the premium end
- Push trolleys are lighter and more compact than electric models; easier to store at home and in a car boot (source: multiple 2026 buyer guides)
- Push trolleys typically include more integrated storage (umbrella holder, drinks holder, scorecard slot) as standard; electric models often sell these as add-on accessories
- Electric trolleys are significantly heavier due to motor and battery hardware, so a smooth, compact fold matters more when evaluating them
- Battery types: lithium is the standard to look for — lighter and longer-lasting than older lead-acid; 18-hole lithium covers a standard round, 27/36-hole batteries suit hilly courses or back-to-back rounds
- Key electric brands in the UK market: Motocaddy and PowaKaddy dominate; also Hill Billy (UK-built), Stewart Golf at the premium/follow end
- Key push trolley names cited in 2026 guides: PowaKaddy Micra (noted as a best-seller at approx. £189, 7.5 kg), Clicgear 4.0 (approx. £219, Swiss-engineered, aircraft-grade aluminium, noted as still performing after 5+ seasons), Motocaddy QB2, Motocaddy Z1 (ultra-compact fold), PowaKaddy DLX-Lite FF, Benross Slider 2.0, Stewart R1-S
- Electric trolley price range: entry-level from around £499 (e.g. Motocaddy SE), mid-range around £749 (PowaKaddy CT6), flagship with GPS touchscreen at £1,249+ (PowaKaddy CT12 GPS); remote/follow models (e.g. Stewart Golf Q Follow) towards £1,600-£1,900
- Push trolleys drop below £100 at budget end; quality three-wheel models typically £149-£219
- Electric trolleys most practical for golfers who play regularly (to justify cost) and on hilly courses; push trolleys well-suited to flatter courses or less frequent walkers
- Deciding factors summarised across sources: course terrain (hilly vs flat), frequency of play, budget, storage/transport constraints
